summary: The only way to test whether the sixth-century anathemas describe Evagrius is to read them beside the Kephalaia Gnostica, and the check is possible because Guillaumont edited two Syriac versions of that book in 1958. In the longer, unexpurgated version (S2), five chapters (2.17, 3.15, 4.18, 4.80, 5.11) line up with the fourteenth, eleventh, eighth, ninth and fifth anathemas, in some cases almost word for word. In the shorter version (S1) the same chapters are reworded or replaced, which is what an editor who wanted to remove those lines would do. In the three cases I checked where a Greek quotation survives next to differing S1 and S2 wordings (2.64, 2.69, 6.16), the Greek agrees with S2; that kind of evidence is the core of Guillaumont's case that S2 is the original, though the Greek covers only a small part of the book. Casiday argues the opposite: S1 is Evagrius's own text and S2 a later reworking, in which case the matching lines come from the sixth-century Origenists the anathemas were aimed at, not from Evagrius. Ramelli accepts S2 but says the condemned ideas were not Evagrius's own either. Evagrius's Letter to Melania speaks of 'names and numbers' being taken away at the end, but adds that the Father, Son and Spirit do not vanish and that creation has a beginning, and readers differ on how far that qualification governs the rest. I could not see Guillaumont's own table of pairings, so the five pairs rest on a personal web essay, checked by me against the text, and every reading of a scholar here comes at second hand.

passages.english:
Anathema 14 (NPNF; quoted fragments as returned by the fetch tool, rest my summary): all rational beings will one day be united in one, so that bodies, separate existences and names disappear; 'the knowledge of the world to come will carry with it the ruin of the worlds'; 'the abolition of [all] names'; 'an identity of the γνῶσις and of the hypostasis'.
KG 2.17, S2 (Dysinger, public domain): Accompanying the knowledge that concerns the logikoi are the destruction of worlds, the dissolution of bodies, and the abolition of names; while [there] remains the equality of knowledge according to the equality of substances.
KG 2.17, S1 (own translation from the Syriac, provisional): 'In the schooling (or nurture) of the knowledge of the rational beings, worlds are exchanged and names are released, while equality of knowledge remains, like the equality of persons (qnumē).'
passages.english_source: S2: Luke Dysinger (public domain). S1 and the anathema summary: own translation. Standard published translation of S2 for comparison: Ramelli, SBL 2015.
passages.textual_notes: (1) The two Syriac versions differ here. S2 has three losses: 'ruin' (ḥablā) of worlds, 'dissolution' of bodies, and the 'abolition' of names; S1 has worlds 'exchanged' and names 'released' and says nothing of bodies. My S1 translation is provisional; the first word (b-tarbītā, 'in the nurture/schooling of') is the least sure. (2) Dysinger's 'substances' renders Syriac qnumē, the ordinary Syriac word for 'hypostases'; this is the word the anathema's 'identity of ... hypostasis' matches. Dysinger's 'logikoi' stands for mallilē, literally 'speaking ones' (rational beings). (3) I could not check how far the Syriac noun ʿṭāyā ('abolition' in Dysinger, following Guillaumont's French) can also mean 'covering'; what looks like the same root is used in the Great Letter, section 23 (mtʿṭyn), where Frankenberg's Greek has ἀφανίζονται, 'are made to vanish'. That link is my own observation and the Syriac lexicon was not checked. (4) Nothing in the Greek fragments I opened corresponds to this chapter, so S2 against S1 cannot be tested here by Greek.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the closest verbal match I found between the 553 list and Evagrius. If S2 is Evagrius's own text, the fourteenth anathema names an Evagrian sentence. If S2 is a later reworking, the sentence belongs to the sixth-century Origenists the anathema was aimed at. On either view it is not a sentence of Origen's.

passages.english:
Anathema 8 (NPNF; quoted fragments as returned by the fetch tool, rest my summary): condemns anyone who will not confess that God the Word is Christ in every sense, and holds instead that the intelligence (nous) united to the Word is Christ, that 'the Logos is only called Christ because of this union with the intelligence, and e converso that the intelligence is only called God because of the Logos'.
KG 4.18, S2 (Dysinger, public domain): The intelligible anointing is the spiritual knowledge of the holy Unity, and the Christ is he who is united to this knowledge. And if this is so, the Christ is not the Word in the beginning, just as he who is anointed is not God in the beginning. Rather the latter [God] because of the former [anointed] is the Christ, and the former [anointed] because of the latter [God] is God.
KG 4.18, S1 (own translation from the Syriac): 'Intelligible anointing is knowledge of the holy Unity. The teacher of this to the rational beings is the Lord Christ.'
passages.english_source: S2: Luke Dysinger (public domain). S1 and anathema summary: own translation. Comparison: Ramelli, SBL 2015.
passages.textual_notes: (1) S1 keeps the first sentence and then says something quite different: Christ is the teacher of this knowledge. The S2 sentences that the eighth anathema echoes are not in S1 at all. (2) The S2 Syriac reads literally 'the Word is not Christ at first (qadmāyt), as he who was anointed is not God at first; but that one because of this one is Christ, and this one because of that one is God'. The demonstratives are ambiguous; Dysinger resolves them as [God]/[the anointed] and turns the first clause round ('the Christ is not the Word'). The adverb qadmāyt ('at first, originally') matters: the claim concerns what the two are at the start. (3) Syriac yaḥidāyūtā, 'Unity', corresponds to Greek μονάς where Greek survives: KG 5.84 in the Greek fragments has ὁ τῆς ἁγίας μονάδος θεατής, 'beholder of the holy monad'. (4) 'Anointing' (mshiḥūtā) and 'Christ' (mshiḥā) share one root in Syriac, which makes the wordplay of the chapter easier to see than in Greek.
passages.why_it_matters: The eighth anathema describes a Christ who is a created mind united to the Word. This chapter is the clearest place in Evagrius for that picture, and it is exactly what the expurgating editor removed from S1.

passages.english:
Anathema 9 (NPNF; quoted fragment as returned by the fetch tool, rest my summary): '...that it was not the Divine Logos made man by taking an animated body...' The anathema condemns saying that the intelligence (nous), and not the Divine Logos, became man, descended into hell and ascended into heaven.
KG 4.80, S2 (Dysinger, public domain): It is not the Word of God who descended to Sheol and ascended to Heaven, but the Christ, who has the Word [with]in Him; indeed, the coarse body is not receptive of knowledge, and God is known.
KG 4.80, S1 (own translation from the Syriac): 'The descent of our Lord to Sheol and his ascent to the Father was not for his own sake but for ours. For his nature had no need of this; his love alone brought him to it.'
passages.english_source: S2: Luke Dysinger (public domain). S1 and anathema summary: own translation. The last verb of S1 (ʾasnqeh) is uncertain to me; 'brought him to it' is a guess at 'compelled' or 'led'.
passages.textual_notes: (1) The S2 Syriac has the adverb qadmāyt ('first, at first') after 'Word of God'; Dysinger's English leaves it out, and I cannot tell whether it qualifies 'Word of God' or the verbs. (2) S1 replaces the chapter. It keeps the descent and ascent but says nothing of who went down: Christ's love, not his nature's need, is the cause. (3) The pair is looser than 2.17 and 4.18: the anathema has an animated body and an intelligence; the chapter has a coarse body that cannot receive knowledge, and Christ as the one who has the Word within him.
passages.why_it_matters: The ninth anathema is about who the subject of Christ's descent is. S2 gives Evagrius an answer that separates 'Christ' (the anointed mind) from 'the Word'; S1 hides the question. Whether the answer is Evagrius's own or a later hand's is the S1/S2 dispute in small.

passages.english:
Anathema 5 (NPNF; quoted fragment as returned by the fetch tool, rest my summary): 'If anyone shall say that a psychic (ψυχικὴν) condition has come from an angelic or archangelic state...' The anathema condemns the teaching that rational beings pass from angelic to psychic to demonic or human states, and back again.
KG 5.11, S2 (Dysinger, public domain): From the order of angels come the order of archangels and that of psychics; from that of psychics (will come that) of demons and of men; and from that of men will come anew that of angels and demons, if a demon is that which, because of an abundance of thumos, has fallen the praktike and has been joined to a darkened and extensive body.
KG 5.11, S1: not given in a close translation. As I read it, S1 speaks of the ordering of the angels training men in human conduct, of demons being brought down, and of those who strive upward passing over the ranks from which they fell. The cycle angels, archangels, souls, demons and men, then angels again, is not there (own gist; Syriac partly uncertain).

passages.textual_notes: (1) 'Psychics' in Dysinger is Syriac napšānē, 'soul-beings': the order of souls between archangels and men. The anathema's Greek word is ψυχική. passages.english:
Anathema 11 (NPNF; quoted fragment as returned by the fetch tool, rest my summary): 'If anyone shall say that the future judgment signifies the destruction of the body...' The anathema condemns teaching that the end of all things is a purely immaterial nature.
KG 3.15, S2 (Dysinger, public domain): If the perfection of the nous is immaterial knowledge, as it is said, and if immaterial knowledge is solely the Trinity, it is evident that in perfection there will not remain anything of matter. And if that is so, the nous, forevermore naked will come to vision of the Trinity.
KG 3.66, S2 (Dysinger): Just as the first trumpet has made known the genesis of bodies, so in the same way will ‘the last trumpet’ make known the destruction of bodies.
KG 3.15, S1 (own translation from the Syriac, provisional): 'If the perfection of the mind is knowledge of spirit, as the Fathers say, and its crown is knowledge of the holy Trinity, it is evident that whoever lacks any of this is far from perfection.'
passages.english_source: S2: Luke Dysinger (public domain). S1 and anathema summary: own translation ('crown' for kelīlā is a guess; it may mean 'complete').
passages.textual_notes: (1) S2 says 'immaterial knowledge' (yāʿūtā lā hūlānītā, 'knowledge without matter') where S1 says 'knowledge of spirit' (yāʿūtā d-rūḥā) and appeals to 'the Fathers'. S2's last clause, that the mind will 'henceforth be a naked seer of the Trinity', has no counterpart in S1. (2) The destruction of bodies in 3.66 (S2) uses the same noun ḥablā ('ruin') that 2.17 uses of worlds. (3) The eleventh anathema is about the judgment, and Evagrius's chapters speak of the final contemplation; the match is thematic, not verbal.
passages.why_it_matters: The idea that bodies drop away and the mind ends 'naked' before the Trinity is the heart of the eleventh anathema. Whether it is Evagrius's (S2) or a sixth-century addition (S1 original) bears directly on whom that anathema condemns.

passages.title: Beings before the judgment: where S1, S2 and a Greek quotation meet (Kephalaia Gnostica 2.64 and 2.69)
passages.author_work_ref: Evagrius of Pontus, Kephalaia Gnostica 2.64 and 2.69; Greek preserved in Barsanuphius and John of Gaza, Letters (2.64 under letter marker 600)
passages.language: Syriac S2 and S1; Greek quotation
passages.original:
Greek 2.64 (second half only): Περὶ μὲν τῶν προτέρων ὁ μηνύσων οὐδείς, περὶ δὲ τῶν δευτέρων ὁ ἐν Χωρὴβ ἐξηγήσατο.
Greek 2.69: Τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον οὐ τὴν πρώτην τῶν λογικῶν διαίρεσιν, οὐδὲ τὴν πρώτην οὐσίαν τῶν σωμάτων ἐξηγήσατο.

Syriac S1 2.64: ܓܠܝܢܐ ܕܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܕܗ̣ܘܐ܆ ܠܐ ܟܬܝܒܐ ܗܘ ܘܟܬܝܒܐ. ܠܐ ܟܬܝܒܐ܆ ܗ̇ܘ ܕܡܢ ܪܘܚܐ ܠ̇ܗܘܢܐ ܡܬܓ̣ܠܐ. ܟܬܝܒܐ ܕܝܢ܆ ܗ̇ܘ ܕܒܝܕ ܪܘܚܐ ܒܚܘܪܝܒ ܐܬܝܗܒ܀
(Syriac of 2.69 in both versions is in the two files; not copied here.)

passages.english:
KG 2.64, S2 (Dysinger, public domain): Among the beings some have been produced before the judgement, and others after the judgement. And as regards the subject of the first [beings], no one has provided information, but as regards the subject of the second [beings], he who has been on Horeb has given an account.
KG 2.64, Greek (own translation): 'Concerning the first, there is no one to inform; concerning the second, the one on Horeb explained.'
KG 2.64, S1 (own translation from the Syriac): 'The revelation of everything that has come to be is both unwritten and written. The unwritten is what is revealed to the mind by the Spirit; the written is what was given by the Spirit on Horeb.'
KG 2.69, S2 (Dysinger): It is not the first distinction of the logikoi and the genesis of bodies that the Holy Spirit has made know to us; but it is, rather, the present distinction between the logikoi and the transformation of bodies that He has revealed us.
KG 2.69, Greek (own translation): 'The Holy Spirit did not explain the first division of the rational beings, nor the first substance of bodies.'
KG 2.69, S1 (own translation, provisional): 'The Holy Spirit through Moses revealed to us nothing about heavenly distinctions, but investigated for us the distinctions of beings in this world.'
passages.english_source: S2: Luke Dysinger (public domain). Greek, S1: own translations; compare Ramelli 2015 for S2.
passages.textual_notes: (1) S1 and S2 give two different chapters under 2.64. S2 says some beings were produced 'before the judgment' and others 'after', and that Moses (the one on Horeb) wrote only of the second. S1 says nothing of a judgment or of two kinds of beings; it speaks of written and unwritten revelation. (2) The Greek quotation preserves only the second half of 2.64, and it agrees with the S2 half; S1 has nothing like it. The same holds for 2.69: the Greek ('the first division of the rational beings') matches S2, while S1 speaks of 'heavenly distinctions'. (3) The Greek is a quotation in the sixth-century letter-collection of Barsanuphius and John of Gaza. It therefore shows S2-type wording in Greek by the time of the second controversy; it cannot show what Evagrius wrote in the 390s. Ramelli (Brill 2019) notes the Kephalaia in this correspondence; I did not see her treat 2.64. (4) A third case with Greek: KG 6.16. Greek (Furrer-Pilliod 2000) has 'Christ is he who appeared to us (ἡμῖν ἐπιφανείς)... two Christs, or two Sons'. S2 has 'appeared to us' and 'or'; S1 has 'came down to the race of men' and 'and'. I checked this one only against the digital files.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the clearest small test of the S1/S2 question. In the three cases I checked where a Greek quotation survives next to differing S1 and S2 wordings (2.64, 2.69, 6.16), the Greek sides with S2. Where S1 and S2 do not differ (for example KG 3.12) the Greek proves nothing either way. Guillaumont's argument rests on a few dozen cases like this. The objection (Casiday) is that the Greek covers little and may itself come from Origenist circles.

readings.work: Les six centuries des 'Kephalaia gnostica', PO 28.1 (1958); Collège de France, Annuaire (c. 1980-81), report on his teaching (page not known)
readings.position: S1 is a revision that 'a corrigé le texte pour en faire disparaître, ou du moins atténuer le plus possible, les propositions incriminées'; S2 is 'une seconde version syriaque, dont l'auteur a cherché à rétablir le texte dans sa teneur originale'. His chief proof is the Greek fragments (about 75 sentences, per Peretó Rivas), where S2 is consistently the closer.
readings.side: S2 is original; S1 is expurgated

passages.title: When the mind is called God: Kephalaia Gnostica 5.81 in S1 and S2
passages.author_work_ref: Evagrius of Pontus, Kephalaia Gnostica 5.81 (Syriac S2 and S1)
passages.language: Syriac (translation of a lost Greek original); no Greek fragment of this chapter found
passages.original:
S2: ܐܡܬܝ ܕܗܘܢܐ ܢܩ̇ܒܠ ܝܕܥܬܐ ܐܝܬܝܝܬܐ܆ ܗܝܕܝܢ ܐܦ ܐܠܗܐ ܢܬܩܪܐ. ܒܕܡܫܟܚ ܐܦ ܥܠܡ̈ܐ ܡܫܚܠܦ̈ܐ ܢ̇ܬܩܢ܀

Syriac copied by script, no letters altered. Greek text of the anathemas not obtained.
passages.english:
S2 (Dysinger, public domain): When the nous will have received essential knowledge, then it will also be called "God" , because it will also be able to found varied worlds.
S1 (own translation from the Syriac): 'When the mind has been made worthy to be in the contemplation of the holy Unity, then in goodness it is also called God, in that it has been filled with the image of its Creator.'
passages.english_source: S2: Luke Dysinger (public domain). S1: own translation; ܒܛܝܒܘܬܐ (b-ṭaybūtā) can be 'in goodness' or 'by grace'.
passages.textual_notes: (1) The two versions say different things. S2: the mind that has received 'essential knowledge' will be called God because it can also 'found varied worlds'. S1: the mind that contemplates the holy Unity is called God by grace, because it is filled with the image of its Creator. Creating worlds, and 'essential' (substantial) knowledge, are both absent from S1. (2) 'Essential knowledge' (yāʿūtā ʾītāyāytā) is Evagrius's term for the knowledge of the Trinity itself; Greek fragments elsewhere give οὐσιώδης γνῶσις (for example KG 3.12, 6.16). (3) I mark this chapter as bearing on the twelfth and thirteenth anathemas (minds made equal to Christ and the Word) by my own judgement; I did not find a scholar who pairs it with an anathema.
passages.why_it_matters: The phrase 'will be called God' is the most quoted S2-only line on how far Evagrius takes the mind's destiny. It is the case readers cite when they ask whether Evagrius taught that minds become equal to Christ, and the S1 editor's change shows someone in antiquity thought it needed softening.

readings.work: Evagrius Ponticus: The Making of a Gnostic (Farnham: Ashgate, 2009), as cited by Santiago Hernán Vazquez, Estudios Filosóficos 68 (2019), nn. 4 and 70, pp. 345 and 357
readings.position: The intellect can attain essential (substantial) knowledge, which seems synonymous with God's essence, but never becomes that essence.
readings.side: reads the S2 language as union by knowledge, not identity of nature

readings.side: reads what was condemned as later Origenism, not Evagrius or Origen

readings.work: Note to his English translation of the Kephalaia (reproduced in the TAN-Evagrius file)
readings.position: Says the expurgated S1 is a re-editing of Evagrius's text 'in which all passages suggestive of controversial Origenist doctrine had either been eliminated or modified'. Chapter 5.81 is not named; it fits the description.
readings.side: S2 is original; S1 is expurgated

readings.position: If S2 is the later text, the 'founding of worlds' clause is the Origenists' addition. General position.
readings.side: reads S2 as possibly a later, sixth-century expansion of S1

passages.english:
Own translation, from the Syriac and checked against Frankenberg's Greek; provisional, since I read Syriac slowly and have not seen a specialist's check.
§22: 'And as there will be a time when these names and numbers are taken away from between the body and the soul and the mind, in that they are raised into the rank of mind, because he gave that they should be one in us, as I and you are one, so there will be a time when names and numbers are taken away from between the Father and his Son and his Spirit and his rational creation, which is his body, so that God may be all in all.'
§23: 'But do not suppose, because I said that names and numbers are taken away between the rational creation and its Creator, that the hypostases and names of the Father and the Son and the Spirit are hidden away too. Rather, as the nature of the mind is united with the nature of the Father, since it is his body, so the names of the soul and the body are swallowed up in the hypostases of the Son and of the Spirit, and one nature remains without end, three hypostases of God and of his image.'
passages.english_source: Own translation. Published English for comparison: Augustine Casiday, Evagrius Ponticus (London: Routledge, 2006), Letter to Melania; Martin Parmentier, 'Evagrius of Pontus' Letter to Melania', Bijdragen 46 (1985), 2-38. German: Gabriel Bunge, 1986.
passages.textual_notes: (1) 'From between': Syriac min bayt X l-Y is the idiom for 'between X and Y'; Frankenberg's Greek has ἐκ μέσου. A literal 'from the house of' would be wrong. (2) The Syriac says 'I and you are one' (John 17); Frankenberg's Greek has 'we'. (3) The phrase 'three hypostases of God and of his image' ends in a damaged place, and the last words of §23 are lost; do not build on them. (4) 'Hidden away' translates mtʿṭyn; Frankenberg's Greek has ἀφανίζονται, 'made to vanish'. (5) The sentence 'names and numbers will be taken away' is easy to read as the anathema's 'abolition of names'; §23 is Evagrius's own warning that this does not mean the three hypostases vanish. Readers differ on how far that warning governs the rest of the letter.
passages.why_it_matters: This letter is the text where Evagrius himself says that names and numbers will be taken away at the end. It is the passage most often set beside the fourteenth anathema, and it shows both what the later condemnation fastened on and what the letter itself guards against.

passages.english:
Own translation, from the Greek retroversion and the Syriac; provisional.
§27 (summary): the minds that return to God do not add a second nature to him. If the visible sea, one in nature, colour and taste, changes the taste of many rivers into its own, how much more will the boundless, unchanging intelligible sea, God the Father, change the minds that return to him like torrents into his own nature, colour and taste. They will be not many but one in union with him.
§29 (end): 'But when the land is taken away from the middle, the sea and the rivers are one, without change. So when sin is removed from between the minds and God, they are one and not many.'
§30: 'But do not suppose, because I said that the rational beings were in God like rivers in the sea from the beginning, that they are without beginning with him by nature. Even if they are with him without beginning in his wisdom and his creating power, their creation has a beginning. But do not reckon an end for them, because of their union with him who has neither beginning nor end.'
passages.english_source: Own translation. For comparison: Casiday 2006; Parmentier 1985; Bunge 1986.
passages.textual_notes: (1) §30 is the letter's own answer to a pre-existence reading: the rational beings are with God without beginning only 'in his wisdom and creating power'; their creation has a beginning. It is also what bears on the fifteenth anathema ('the end ... like the beginning'): the letter says the beginning of creation is real, and that union gives no 'end' to be reckoned. (2) The Syriac of §30 is damaged in two places and has one doubtful word; the Greek reads smoothly because Frankenberg supplied it. (3) 'Taken away' in §29 translates the verb ʾetshqal / ʾetʿṭy; the second is the root discussed in the note to KG 2.17.
passages.why_it_matters: The sea-and-rivers image is the letter's picture of the end: many minds, one sea. Whether it describes union with God by will and grace or a loss of distinct existence is exactly what readers disagree about, and §30 keeps the beginning of creation and the question of an end open.

other_findings.claim: The unexpurgated Syriac S2 and the common, expurgated S1 are both edited in Guillaumont, Patrologia Orientalis 28.1 (1958), and survive in the digital TAN-Evagrius repository (Kalvesmaki), together with Dysinger's English of S2, which the file calls public domain.

Guillaumont's 1962 book and his 1961 article 'Évagre et les anathématismes anti-origénistes de 553' (Studia Patristica 3, pp. 219-226) are where the anathemas are set against the Kephalaia. I did not see either; only quotations of them in Ramelli's 2015 introduction (p. xxvi n. 55 and p. xxxvii n. 96).

Castellano's web essay also lists Kephalaia parallels for anathemas 2 (3.22, 1.49-50, 3.45, 6.75, 2.66, 2.76, 2.14, 6.78, 6.80, 1.63), 3 (1.63, 6.88, 3.37, 3.84, 4.29, 3.62), 6 (5.11, 3.23), 7 (2.24, 6.33, 4.41), 10 (4.24, 6.34) and 12 (3.15, 3.12, 6.34). I read the S2 English of some of them; the matches are looser than for anathemas 5, 8, 9, 11 and 14, and I have not set them out.

The same essay says the sixth-century opponents were quoting the Kephalaia from the Origenists to the council, and cites Diekamp (1899) for the bishops' assent before the council opened. Those are the essay's claims, unchecked here.

Casiday (2013) argues S1 is Evagrius's own text and S2 a later expansion, partly because an Armenian version of about 450 rests on S1. Peretó Rivas (Stylos 2015) finds the case stronger than Guillaumont's; his 2019 Adamantius article revisits the question (abstract only seen).

Guillaumont's report to the Collège de France (c. 1980-81) describes S1 as correcting the text 'pour en faire disparaître, ou du moins atténuer le plus possible, les propositions incriminées' and S2 as the work of an author who 'a cherché à rétablir le texte dans sa teneur originale'. It calls the Letter to Melania Evagrius's most important letter, preserved in Syriac.

Greek fragments of the Kephalaia survive in Barsanuphius and John's letters (Ramelli notes 'Ep. 600'), in Hausherr 1939, Muyldermans 1931-32, Géhin 1996 and Furrer-Pilliod 2000; Peretó Rivas says Guillaumont relied on about 75 sentences.

Gabriel Bunge's 1986 German translation of the Great Letter (Briefe aus der Wüste) is the only complete modern translation with full notes, according to Baán (2022 n. 4); Bunge proposes that Rufinus, not Melania, was the real addressee (Baán n. 4; Ramelli 2015 p. xxx n. 72).
Frankenberg published the first part of the Great Letter, to section 31, from manuscript A; Baán's notes give pp. 610-619 and disagree on whether the text ends at §31 or §34.

Ramelli reads Evagrius as 'an Origenian ... more than an Origenist', perfectly orthodox on the Trinity, and says the doctrines condemned from 553 on were 'largely neither those of Origen nor those of Evagrius' (SBL 2015, pp. xxv-xxvii). Her page numbers come from a fetch-tool summary of the open-access PDF and should be checked in the book.

problems: (1) I did not obtain Guillaumont's own table of anathemas against Kephalaia chapters (1962 book; 1961 Studia Patristica article). The persée reviews were blocked to my fetch tool and archive.org, Google Books and the publishers were not reachable, so every pair above comes from Castellano's web essay (which follows Fr Theophanes of Mount Athos), checked by me against the S2 text. I cannot say which pairs are on Guillaumont's list, and the pairing is S at best. Page numbers for Guillaumont 1962 are unconfirmed. (2) The Greek text of the fifteen anathemas (Diekamp 1899, Mansi IX 395-400) was not found. The NPNF English could only be read in fragments of about 125 characters through a fetch tool, so the anathema side of each pair is partly my summary. (3) None of the five paired KG chapters (2.17, 4.18, 4.80, 5.11, 3.15) has a Greek fragment in the digital Greek files I opened (Géhin 1996, Hausherr 1939, Muyldermans 1932, Furrer-Pilliod 2000, Devreesse, de Angelis-Noah/Neyt, and others); the 1931 Muyldermans file was not retrievable. Greek exists for 2.64 (second half), 2.69, 6.16, 3.12 and a few other chapters. (4) The Syriac is a digital transcription of Guillaumont's printed text, not the printed text; page markers in it may be off by one. No Syriac typed from memory. My translations of S1 and of the Letter to Melania are provisional and unchecked by a Syriac reader. (5) The Great Letter is only partly in the digital Syriac (to §31, with gaps); the Greek is Frankenberg's modern retroversion. Casiday 2006 and Parmentier 1985 were not available, so I could not report what they say about §§22-30. (6) Several scholars on the brief (Bunge, Corrigan, Stewart, Young, Konstantinovsky on these chapters, Daley on specific chapters, Misiarczyk beyond his abstract) could not be shown to discuss these exact passages. Where I could not attribute a reading with confidence I left it out; Bunge appears only for his 1986 translation. (7) Every scholarly reading is S: taken from a fetch tool's summary of the source or a report of it, not from my own reading of the whole work. Page numbers given for Ramelli 2015, Vazquez 2019, Baán 2022 and Peretó Rivas 2015 are as the tool reported them.
